mishnayot.title: A harmless ox that gores several oxen
mishnayot.summary: A harmless ox pays only from its own body. When it gored several oxen in turn, Rabbi Meir has the last victim paid first; Rabbi Shimon has the victims share.

b: An ox gored four or five oxen, one after another. The owner pays the owner of the last ox injured; if money remains, the one before; and so on. The last benefits, according to Rabbi Meir.

An ox worth 200 gored an ox worth 200 and the carcass is worth nothing: each owner gets 100. If it gores a third worth 200: the last gets 100, the previous 50. A fourth: the last 100, the previous 50, and the first two 25 each.

Rabbi Meir: the injured owner seized the ox to collect his half damages and so became its paid guard; if it then gores again, the later victim is paid from what remains of it. Rabbi Shimon: the injured owner and the ox's owner become partners in it.
The Gemara: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yishmael (the injured is a creditor of the damager), Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Akiva (the injured becomes a partner in the ox).

mishnayot.title: An attested danger for some things only
mishnayot.summary: An ox can be an attested danger to one kind of victim and harmless to another, or on one day and not another. For the first it pays full damages, for the other half.

b: An ox that is an attested danger to its own kind but not to others, to people but not to beasts, to children but not to adults: for that for which it is an attested danger, full damages; for the rest, half.
An ox attested as a danger to its own kind (for example, to gore oxen) is not thereby attested as a danger to other kinds.
For example, an ox seen standing with horses and camels and not goring is not an attested danger to those.
Rabbi Judah: an ox that is an attested danger on the Sabbath but not during the week pays full damages for Sabbaths and half damages for weekdays.
It becomes harmless again after it refrains from injury for three Sabbath days.

mishnayot.title: Property of the Temple, of a gentile
mishnayot.summary: An Israelite's ox that gores a sacred ox or a gentile's ox is exempt. A gentile's ox that gores an Israelite's pays full damages, harmless or not.

b: An Israelite's ox that gored an ox of the Temple, or the Temple's that gored an Israelite's: exempt, since the verse says "his neighbour's ox" (Exodus 21:35), not the Temple's.
An Israelite's ox that gored a gentile's: exempt. A gentile's ox that gored an Israelite's, harmless or not: full damages.

For the gentile cases Kehati gives reasons: the Gemara says the seven commandments of Noah were not kept by the nations, so their property was released to Israel; Rambam says it is a fine, since gentiles do not guard against damage; Meiri says it applies to nations not bound by religious norms.

mishnayot.title: Oxen of a deaf-mute, a person with psychosis, a minor
mishnayot.summary: The owner of a sound ox who injures the ox of a deaf-mute, person with psychosis or minor pays. Their ox that injures a sound person's ox: exempt. The court appoints a guardian.

b: An ox of a person of sound senses that gored the ox of a deaf-mute, person with psychosis or minor: obligated. The reverse: exempt.
If their ox gored, the court appoints a guardian, and the ox is warned in front of him.
If the deaf-mute becomes of sound senses, the person with psychosis recovers, or the minor comes of age: Rabbi Meir says the ox is harmless again; Rabbi Yose says it remains as it was.
The Gemara gives Rabbi Meir's reason: a change of owner changes the ox's status.
An ox trained for the stadium is not liable to death, as it says "when it will gore" and not "when others cause it to gore".

mishnayot.title: An ox that kills a person
mishnayot.summary: An ox that kills a person is stoned. An attested danger's owner also pays ransom; a harmless ox's owner does not. For a slave, thirty sela.

b: An ox gored a person and he died: if it was an attested danger, its owner pays the ransom (kofer); if harmless, he is exempt from it. In both cases the ox is put to death.
The same for a son or a daughter. For a male or female slave: its owner pays 30 sela, whether the slave was worth a maneh or not a dinar.

An attested-danger ox that kills a person is stoned and its owner pays ransom (kofer) to the heirs (Exodus 21:28-30). A harmless ox is stoned but its owner pays no kofer, since the Torah ordered kofer only for an attested danger.
Kofer is the value of the person killed.

mishnayot.title: An ox that did not intend to kill
mishnayot.summary: An ox is judged by its intention. If it did not mean to kill a person, it is exempt from death.

b: An ox rubbing against a wall that fell on a person; an ox that intended to kill an animal and killed a man; one that intended to kill a gentile and killed an Israelite; one that intended to kill an untimely birth and killed a viable infant: exempt from death.
In each case the ox did not intend to kill a person whose killing carries death, so it is not put to death.

mishnayot.title: Oxen of those with no adult male owner
mishnayot.summary: The ox of a woman, orphans, a guardian, or a wild, Temple or convert's ownerless ox that kills is put to death. Rabbi Judah exempts the ones with no owner. The halakha does not follow him.

b: The ox of a woman, of orphans, of a guardian, a wild ox, an ox of the Temple, or of a convert who died without heirs: all are liable to death.
Rabbi Judah: a wild ox, a Temple ox and a convert's ox are exempt, since they have no owners.
Rabbi Judah looks at the time of judgment: if the ox then has no owner it is exempt, even if it gored while it had one.
The halakha does not follow Rabbi Judah.

mishnayot.title: Dedicating an ox that is going to be stoned
mishnayot.summary: An owner cannot dedicate or slaughter an ox once sentence is complete. Before that, his act is valid.

b: If an ox goes out to be stoned and its owners dedicate it, it is not dedicated. If he slaughtered it, its flesh is forbidden.
If before its sentence was complete its owner dedicated it, it is dedicated; if he slaughtered it, its flesh is permitted.
The mishnah teaches from when the owners lose their power over an ox that killed: once its sentence is complete they have no right to dedicate it.
After the sentence the flesh is forbidden to eat and to benefit from.

mishnayot.title: Guards, and an ox that was properly guarded
mishnayot.summary: A guard takes the owner's place. If the owner tied or locked the ox properly and it still damaged, the sages dispute: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Judah and Rabbi Eliezer. The halakha follows Rabbi Judah.

outline.h: A guard takes the owner's place
b: If one handed it to an unpaid guardian, a borrower, a paid guardian or a hirer, they take the place of the owners: full damages for an attested danger, half for a harmless one.
If its owner tied it with a halter or locked it up properly, but it came out and caused damage: Rabbi Meir: liable, whether an attested danger or harmless.
Rabbi Judah: if harmless he is liable; if an attested danger he is exempt, as it says "and its owner did not guard it", but this one was guarded.
Rabbi Eliezer: its only guarding is the knife.
Rabbi Judah's exemption is from the full payment: the owner still pays half damages.

There are three views about an attested danger that was guarded: Rabbi Meir: liable if the guard was weak, exempt if strong; Rabbi Judah: exempt from the full payment even with a weak guard; Rabbi Eliezer: liable even with a strong guard.
